content.title: About
content.content: Black beans and white rice is a classic combination found throughout Latin American, Caribbean, and South American cuisines. Beans provide plant‑based protein, fiber, and micronutrients, while rice supplies quick‑digesting carbohydrates and a light texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Black beans are often called the “queen of beans” for their rich flavor and high antioxidant content.
Together beans and rice form a complete protein, offering all essential amino acids similar to animal protein.
In several countries the dish is a national staple and is served on holidays and celebrations.
The dark color of black beans comes from anthocyanins, which have anti‑inflammatory properties.
Traditionally rice is rinsed several times to remove excess starch and improve fluffiness.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Black beans contain about 20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance and satiety.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, helps regulate blood sugar, and promotes heart health.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Anthocyanins in black beans protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Source of iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals are essential for hemoglobin formation and nerve‑muscle function.

items.title: Energy‑dense rice
items.content: White rice quickly supplies glucose, making it useful after physical activity.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Beans contain phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption; soaking and sprouting lower its level.

items.title: High glycemic index of rice
items.content: White rice can raise blood sugar rapidly; people with diabetes may prefer whole‑grain rice or control portions.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: A small percentage of individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Gas production
items.content: Beans can cause flatulence; proper preparation (soaking, thorough cooking) mitigates this effect.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook beans and rice together in a 1:2 ratio, adding spices, vegetables, or meat. They are used in salads, casseroles, soups, and as a side dish. Soak dry beans at least 6 hours before boiling until tender.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry place for up to 1 year. Cooked beans and prepared rice keep 3–4 days in the refrigerator and up to 3 months in the freezer.

chicken-fillet-sandwich-fried-from-fast-.title: Chicken Fillet Sandwich, Fried, with Cheese

content.title: About
content.content: The chicken fillet sandwich is a staple item in fast‑food menus. A juicy piece of fried chicken fillet is placed between a soft bun, topped with melted cheese, fresh vegetables, and sauce. It is quick to prepare, easy to carry, and offers a balance of protein and carbohydrates.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Typical serving weight ranges from 150 to 200 g.
Frying the fillet in oil gives it a golden crust and a crunchy texture.
The cheese is usually processed, which speeds up melting during assembly.
Some locations season the fillet with paprika or garlic powder for extra flavor.
The sandwich is especially popular with children and teenagers due to its soft texture and mild spice level.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Chicken fillet provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat contains niacin, vitamin B6, and B12, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The sandwich supplies iron, zinc, and phosphorus, important for immunity and bone health.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Carbohydrates from the bun combined with fats from the cheese deliver a quick source of energy.

items.title: Satiety
items.content: A balanced mix of protein, fat, and carbs helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Frying and cheese add calories; those watching weight should control portion size.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Cheese and frying oil contain saturated fats, which can affect cholesterol levels if consumed excessively.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Cheese and sauces are often salty; people with hypertension should opt for lower‑salt versions.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese may trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich is designed to be eaten by hand, but it can be halved for a neater bite. It pairs well with french fries, coleslaw, or fresh veggie sticks. Optional condiments include mustard, ketchup, or a spicy sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Best enjoyed immediately. If needed, keep the sandwich refrigerated for no more than 2 hours, wrapped in foil or plastic wrap to retain bun softness and prevent drying out.

crab-salad-made-with-imitation-crab.title: Crab Salad Made with Imitation Crab

content.title: About
content.content: Crab salad made with imitation crab is prepared from crab sticks (surimi), mayonnaise, fresh vegetables and seasonings. Imitation crab is produced from fish paste, starch, egg white and flavorings, mimicking the taste and texture of real crab meat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Crab sticks were invented in Japan in the 1970s as a cheap alternative to real crab.
Imitation crab typically contains about 60 % fish, the rest being starch, egg white and flavor enhancers.
Crab salads are popular in Asia, Europe and North America as a quick picnic dish.
In Russia, crab salad is often served as a festive appetizer.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Imitation crab has less saturated fat than real seafood, making the salad lighter.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Crab sticks provide about 8 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The product contains vitamin B12 and B6, important for nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It supplies iodine, zinc and selenium, which aid thyroid health and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: The soft texture of imitation crab is gentle on the stomach, suitable for people with sensitive digestion.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Imitation crab contains fish, so it can trigger allergic reactions in fish‑allergic individuals.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Crab sticks are often salted; people monitoring sodium intake should watch portion size.

items.title: Additives and flavorings
items.content: The product may contain artificial flavorings and preservatives that some consumers prefer to avoid.

items.title: Calorie‑dense mayonnaise
items.content: Traditional recipes use mayonnaise, which adds significant calories and fat.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled as an appetizer or light meal. It pairs well with bread, toast, rice crackers, or can be used as a filling for sushi rolls.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Do not leave imitation crab at room temperature for more than 4 hours.

iced-tea-lemonade-juice-drink-light.title: Iced Tea / Lemonade Juice Drink, Light

content.title: About
content.content: Iced Tea / Lemonade Juice Drink, Light is a refreshing non‑alcoholic beverage that blends aromatic tea with a light lemonade note. The drink is low in sugar, low‑calorie, and suitable for those watching their diet while still enjoying flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The base is black or green tea, providing a mild astringency and antioxidants.
Lemon juice adds vitamin C and natural tartness without artificial flavorings.
The light version contains about 30 kcal per 100 ml, roughly half the calories of typical sugary sodas.
It is often served over ice with fresh mint to enhance the refreshing effect.
In some countries it is known as “tea‑lemonade” and is a staple of summer café menus.

items.title: Tea antioxidants
items.content: Tea is rich in polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Vitamin C from lemon
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids iron absorption.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: The light version fits well into calorie‑restricted diets, allowing enjoyment without excess energy.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: High water content helps maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: No artificial colors
items.content: The product typically contains no synthetic colorants, making it more natural.

items.title: Caffeine
items.content: Tea contains caffeine, which may cause insomnia or increased heart rate in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Lemon juice raises the drink’s acidity, which can irritate the stomach if consumed in large amounts.

items.title: Citrus allergy
items.content: People allergic to citrus may react to the lemon component.

items.title: Sugar content in some variants
items.content: Despite the “light” label, some brands add a small amount of sugar; always check the label.

content.title: How to Enjoy
content.content: Serve chilled over ice, garnish with a lemon slice or a sprig of mint. Add fresh berries for extra flavor if desired. The drink works as a standalone refresher or as a base for non‑alcoholic cocktails.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 2–4 °C. Once opened, consume within 3–5 days. Avoid prolonged exposure to direct sunlight to preserve flavor and color.

content.title: About
content.content: Lamb chop is a cut taken from the rib section of a lamb or sheep, usually 2–3 cm thick. It has a rich, slightly sweet flavor and a tender texture, especially when cooked properly.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lamb has been consumed since ancient times and is one of the oldest domesticated meats.
Chops are often marinated in herbs, spices, and yogurt to enhance tenderness.
In many cultures lamb is a symbol of celebration and hospitality.
Lamb contains more iron than beef, making it beneficial for preventing anemia.
Lamb is a good source of conjugated linoleic acid (CLA), which may support heart health.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Lamb provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: The iron in lamb is highly bioavailable and helps maintain healthy hemoglobin levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Lamb supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, important for nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Beneficial fats
items.content: It contains omega‑3 and omega‑6 polyunsaturated fatty acids that support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Essential minerals
items.content: Besides iron, lamb is a good source of zinc and selenium, which boost immunity.

items.title: High saturated fat
items.content: Excessive consumption may raise cholesterol levels.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to lamb.

items.title: Pathogen risk
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor salmonella or E. coli.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Lamb is high in purines, which can be problematic for people with gout.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chops can be grilled, oven‑roasted, or pan‑seared. A common preparation is to marinate them in olive oil, garlic, rosemary, and lemon juice for at least 30 minutes. Cook to an internal temperature of 63 °C for medium‑rare.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh lamb chops refrigerated at 0–4 °C for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze them in an airtight bag at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Thaw frozen chops in the refrigerator before cooking.

meat-loaf-made-with-beef-and-pork-with-t.title: Meat loaf made with beef and pork, with tomato-based sauce

content.title: About
content.content: Meat loaf is prepared from a mixture of beef and pork, baked in the oven and served with a tomato‑based sauce. This hearty dish is common in many cuisines and is often accompanied by potatoes or vegetables.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomatoes give the sauce a bright color and rich flavor while adding vitamin C.
Combining beef and pork yields a softer texture than using a single type of meat.
Meat loaf is traditionally shaped into a rectangular loaf for easy slicing.
Some recipes add breadcrumbs or rolled oats to retain moisture.
Typical seasonings include garlic, paprika, oregano, and black pepper.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Beef and pork provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Red meat contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Lycopene in tomato sauce
items.content: Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that helps protect cells from oxidative damage.

items.title: Satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and fat promotes a lasting feeling of fullness.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Both beef and pork can contain notable amounts of saturated fat, so moderation is advised.

items.title: Sodium in the sauce
items.content: Tomato sauce is often seasoned with salt; people monitoring sodium intake should control portion size.

items.title: Spice allergies
items.content: Some individuals may be sensitive to garlic, paprika, or other spices used in the recipe.

items.title: Proper cooking
items.content: Undercooked meat may harbor harmful bacteria; ensure the internal temperature reaches at least 71 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the meat loaf into portions and serve hot with the tomato sauce. It pairs well with mashed potatoes, rice, fresh vegetables, or a green salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the cooked loaf to room temperature, then place it in an airtight container and refrigerate for 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze individual slices – up to 2 months.

pork-chop-coated-lean-and-fat-eaten.title: Pork chop, coated, lean and fat, edible

content.title: About
content.content: Coated pork chops can include both lean and fattier cuts of meat. The coating is usually a mixture of flour, egg and breadcrumbs, giving the dish a crunchy crust. These chops are commonly pan‑fried or baked and are a popular dish in many cuisines around the world.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pork is one of the most widely consumed meats globally.
The coating helps retain juices inside the meat, making it more tender.
In Russia, coated pork chops are traditionally served with mashed potatoes or buckwheat.
Japan’s version, tonkatsu, is a breaded pork cutlet served with tonkatsu sauce.
Fattier pork contains more vitamin B12 and iron than lean cuts.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Pork provides all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat is high in thiamine, riboflavin, niacin and vitamin B12, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Iron, zinc and phosphorus in pork contribute to healthy blood and bones.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: Fattier portions contain monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that can be heart‑friendly in moderation.

items.title: Satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and fat provides lasting fullness.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Fatty cuts may raise cholesterol levels if eaten frequently.

items.title: Foodborne infection risk
items.content: Undercooked pork can harbor parasites such as Trichinella.

items.title: Allergy to coating ingredients
items.content: Some people may react to wheat, eggs or dairy used in the breading.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared breaded products often contain added salt, which should be considered for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Dredge the chops in flour, beaten egg and breadcrumbs, then fry until golden or bake at 200 °C for 20‑25 minutes. Serve hot with vegetables, potatoes or a salad. A squeeze of lemon or a mustard‑based sauce adds extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh pork should be kept in the refrigerator at +2‑+4 °C for no more than 2‑3 days. Frozen pork lasts up to 6 months. Thaw frozen meat in the fridge before cooking. Cooked breaded chops are best consumed within 1‑2 days, stored in an airtight container.

content.title: About
content.content: Salisbury steak dinner is a ready‑to‑heat frozen meal that includes a seasoned ground‑beef patty prepared in the classic Salisbury style, served with a savory gravy and a side (usually mashed potatoes or vegetables). It belongs to the NFS (National Food Service) line and is designed for quick microwave or stovetop reheating.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The Salisbury steak was created in the late 19th century by Dr. J. H. Salisbury as a more affordable alternative to a beef filet.
NFS frozen meals are widely used in cafeterias, hotels, and military bases because of their long shelf life.
Each serving provides roughly 350 kcal, making it a convenient balanced‑meal option.
The gravy typically combines beef broth, tomato paste, and spices, giving the dish its distinctive flavor.
The product is sealed in a moisture‑vapor barrier pouch, allowing storage in the freezer for up to 24 months.

items.title: Good source of protein
items.content: The beef patty supplies about 20 g of high‑quality protein, essential for muscle maintenance.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Beef is rich in heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The meal provides vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Vegetable side adds fiber
items.content: The accompanying vegetables contribute dietary fiber, vitamin C, and antioxidants.

items.title: Convenient and quick
items.content: Preparation takes only 3–5 minutes, helping to save time and reduce cooking stress.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: A single serving can contain up to 800 mg of sodium, which should be considered by those monitoring blood pressure.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The gravy may contain wheat flour, making the product unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Need for thorough heating
items.content: Insufficient reheating may leave live bacteria; follow the recommended time and temperature guidelines.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Preservatives are used to extend shelf life, which some consumers may wish to avoid.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the frozen meal directly from the freezer: microwave on high for 3–5 minutes, stirring halfway through to ensure even heating. For a fresher touch, add chopped fresh herbs or a squeeze of lemon before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the meal frozen at –18 °C or lower. Once the package is opened, consume within 24 hours and store the remaining portion in the refrigerator at +4 °C. Do not refreeze.

content.title: About
content.content: Sushi Roll Tuna is a roll made of vinegared rice, nori, fresh tuna, cucumber and avocado, often served with soy sauce, wasabi and pickled ginger. The tuna gives the roll a delicate flavor and a protein‑rich profile, while the vegetables add crunch and freshness.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tuna used in sushi is typically served as sashimi‑only, without any cooking, to preserve its tender taste.
Japanese traditionally serve rolls with soy sauce, wasabi and pickled ginger, which enhance aroma and aid digestion.
Nori seaweed, used for the wrapper, is rich in iodine and B‑vitamins.
Sushi rolls originated in Tokyo in the early 19th century as street food and are now enjoyed worldwide.
The tuna in sushi is often skipjack (blue tuna) or yellowfin, each offering distinct flavor and fat content.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Tuna provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Tuna is a good source of EPA and DHA, which support heart and brain health.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: A tuna roll is generally less calorie‑dense than rolls with fried ingredients or mayonnaise.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Tuna supplies vitamin B12 and niacin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The roll contains selenium, magnesium and potassium, which aid immunity and electrolyte balance.

items.title: Parasite risk
items.content: Raw fish can harbor parasites; only use fish that has been properly inspected and frozen according to safety standards.

items.title: Mercury content
items.content: Tuna may contain mercury; pregnant women and children should limit consumption.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to seafood.

items.title: Sodium in soy sauce
items.content: Soy sauce adds sodium, which may be a concern for people with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The roll is typically eaten with chopsticks, dipped in soy sauce, and optionally topped with a dab of wasabi. Pickled ginger can be consumed between bites to cleanse the palate.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store sushi rolls in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C and consume within 24 hours. For longer storage, freezing is possible, though the rice texture may change.

tea-iced-instant-green-pre-sweetened-wit.title: Tea, iced, instant, green, pre‑sweetened with sugar

content.title: About
content.content: Iced instant green tea is a convenient beverage that prepares in seconds by adding hot or cold water. The tea is already sweetened with sugar, so no extra sweetener is needed. It retains the light aroma of green tea and a refreshing taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green tea is rich in polyphenols, especially catechins, which have antioxidant properties.
Instant tea is travel‑friendly: no need to steep leaves.
Pre‑sweetening makes the drink more appealing to children and those who dislike the bitterness of green tea.
In many countries ready‑to‑drink tea mixes are sold in sachets or powder form.
Traditionally, green tea is considered beneficial for metabolism and mental alertness.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Catechins in green tea help neutralize free radicals, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Metabolism support
items.content: Some studies suggest green tea may boost metabolic rate and aid fat oxidation.

items.title: Improved focus
items.content: A modest amount of caffeine in green tea enhances alertness without a strong “jolt.”

items.title: Blood sugar regulation
items.content: Polyphenols and polysaccharides may help stabilize post‑meal glucose levels.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Diluted with water, instant tea contributes to daily fluid intake.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Pre‑sweetened tea adds extra sugar, which can be problematic for diabetics or those watching weight.

items.title: Caffeine
items.content: Although low, caffeine may cause sleep disturbances or jitteriness in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Tea allergy
items.content: Rarely, some people may experience an allergic reaction to tea components.

items.title: Product quality
items.content: Low‑cost instant teas may contain additives, flavorings, or preservatives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Place 1‑2 sachets (or 1‑2 teaspoons of powder) into 200‑250 ml of hot (80‑90 °C) or cold water, stir until fully dissolved. Optionally add lemon, mint, or ice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the package in a dry, cool place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the sachet tightly sealed to prevent moisture absorption.
